_note: Original text written for INTUITY to the Cambridge B2 First Part 5 specification (about 600 words, six questions in text order: detail, inference, reference, purpose, meaning of a phrase and a final question linking the ending to the opening). Each card is a chunk of the article with the question it answers; `highlight` is the sentence that proves the answer, `why` explains the distractors. Used by the Part 5 practice page.
title: Room to roam
subtitle: Eleven farmers in the Welsh borders have joined their land together to give wildlife a safe route across their valley. Hannah Lowe walked it with the man who started it.

cards.text: Gareth Pryce does not look like a revolutionary. He is sixty-two, wears the same green jacket he has owned since the nineties, and speaks so quietly that I keep having to lean closer to hear him. Yet in this valley he is responsible for the biggest change in farming for a generation. Five years ago, he persuaded ten of his neighbours to stop thinking of their fields as separate kingdoms and to start treating the whole valley as a single home for wildlife. 'Animals don't read maps,' he says. 'A fox has no idea where my land stops and yours begins.'
cards.question: What is the writer's first impression of Gareth?
choices: He seems too old to take on such a large project.
He is unwilling to talk about what he has achieved.
He does not seem like someone who would make major changes.
He cares more about animals than about his neighbours.
cards.highlight: Gareth Pryce does not look like a revolutionary.
cards.why: 'Gareth Pryce does not look like a revolutionary', yet he has changed farming in the valley. He speaks quietly, but nothing suggests he refuses to talk.

cards.text: The idea came to him, he admits, almost by accident. One winter morning he found a dead badger on the road that runs along the bottom of his farm, the third that month. He mentioned it in the village pub, expecting sympathy, and instead got a long lecture from a retired biology teacher about 'islands'. Small patches of woodland, she explained, were like islands in a sea of open fields. Animals trapped on them could not reach food, find partners or escape danger. 'I went home slightly annoyed,' Gareth says. 'Mainly because I knew she was right.'
cards.question: What does Gareth suggest about the conversation in the pub?
choices: He had hoped the teacher would offer to help him.
He found it hard to accept a point he could not argue with.
He did not understand what the teacher meant by 'islands'.
He regretted mentioning the badgers to other people.
cards.highlight: Mainly because I knew she was right.
cards.why: He was annoyed 'mainly because I knew she was right', so the problem was that he could not disagree. He clearly understood her idea, because it led to the whole project.

cards.text: Persuading the neighbours was harder. Farmers in the valley had spent centuries putting up fences and digging ditches to keep things out, and Gareth was now asking them to do the opposite. It meant planting hedges that joined up, leaving wide strips of long grass along the edges of fields and building small tunnels under the farm tracks. Some agreed at once. Others needed years. The last to join was Dilys Morgan, whose family had farmed the top of the valley since 1850. Gareth says he drank eleven cups of tea in her kitchen before she finally said yes.
cards.question: What does 'It' refer to in 'It meant planting hedges that joined up'?
choices: the farmers' habit of keeping animals out
the work done by earlier generations of farmers
the cost of putting up fences and ditches
Gareth's request to let wildlife move across the farms
cards.highlight: Gareth was now asking them to do the opposite. It meant planting hedges that joined up
cards.why: 'It' is what Gareth 'was now asking them to do': the opposite of keeping things out. The fences and ditches are the old way, not what the new plan meant.

cards.text: Whether all this has made any difference is a fair question, and Gareth is careful not to claim too much. What he can show me is the evidence from forty small cameras hidden along the corridor, which take a picture whenever something moves. On his laptop he scrolls through thousands of images: deer, stoats, a family of polecats and an extraordinary number of pheasants, which seem to enjoy posing. In the first year, the cameras recorded badgers on just two farms. Last year they recorded them on all eleven. Not one has been found dead on the road since.
cards.question: Why does the writer mention the cameras?
choices: to show that the project has produced clear results
to suggest that Gareth is more interested in technology than farming
to explain why some animals have not benefited from the corridor
to show that Gareth exaggerates the success of the project
cards.highlight: In the first year, the cameras recorded badgers on just two farms. Last year they recorded them on all eleven.
cards.why: Badgers went from 'just two farms' to 'all eleven', which is real evidence. Gareth 'is careful not to claim too much', so he does not exaggerate.

cards.text: Not everyone in the area is a fan. Some farmers outside the group complain that the long grass looks untidy, and one told a local newspaper that the corridor was 'a motorway for rabbits'. Gareth takes this in good humour. The project has also cost him money, because land left wild is land that grows no crops. 'Yes, I'm poorer on paper,' he says. 'But my soil is healthier, I use fewer chemicals and the bees have come back to the orchard. You can't put all of that in a spreadsheet.' He seems genuinely untroubled by the critics, and slightly amused.
cards.question: What does Gareth mean when he says he is 'poorer on paper'?
choices: He has had to sell part of his farm to pay for the project.
He spends less money on newspapers and paperwork.
His accounts show he earns less, but that is not the whole picture.
He is seriously worried about his finances.
cards.why: The figures show less income, but the benefits are things 'you can't put ... in a spreadsheet'. He seems 'untroubled', so he is not seriously worried.

cards.text: As we reach the top of the valley, the light is fading and Gareth stops by a gap in a hedge. A narrow path, worn flat by small feet, runs through it into Dilys Morgan's field. He crouches down to look at it, saying nothing for almost a minute. Then he stands up, a little stiffly, and tells me that two farms in the next valley have asked to join. They want to connect their hedges to his. 'So it's not eleven any more,' he says quietly. 'And the foxes still have no idea whose land they're on.'
cards.question: What does the end of the article suggest about the project?
choices: It has become too large for Gareth to manage.
It is spreading beyond its borders, just as the animals do.
It has finally won over Dilys Morgan.
It has been less popular in the next valley.
cards.highlight: two farms in the next valley have asked to join
cards.why: New farms 'have asked to join', and the foxes still ignore boundaries, as in the opening line 'Animals don't read maps'. Dilys had already joined earlier in the story.
